input.idea:
AI Agent: Turn Screenshots Into Code.
An educational video explaining how AI coding agents can recreate website interfaces from screenshots. Show how a developer provides a screenshot of a website to an AI agent, which analyzes its visual structure, identifies UI elements, colors, spacing, typography and layout, then generates the corresponding HTML, CSS and React components. The result is a functional webpage that visually resembles the original design.

template.reason: This idea already gives you the pieces Build it fast needs. The result is a working page that looks like the original site, the tool is an AI coding agent, and the steps are screenshot → agent reads the layout → HTML/CSS/React code. Opening on the finished page and then replaying the steps fits the channel's "show it on screen, don't tell it" style. It isn't a 5 because the idea doesn't name a specific agent or say how long the build takes, so pick one (Claude Code works) and time a real run.

hooks.text: I gave an AI agent one screenshot. It built this page.
Turning a website screenshot into working React code.
Screenshot to code explained in three simple steps.

hook.text: I gave an AI agent one screenshot. It built this page.

research.facts:
- Screenshot-to-code tools use "multimodal" AI models, which can read images as well as text. The model looks at a picture of a website and writes front-end code that rebuilds it.
- The popular open-source project "screenshot-to-code" turns screenshots, mockups, Figma designs and even screen recordings into code. It can output HTML + Tailwind, React + Tailwind, Vue + Tailwind, Bootstrap or Ionic.
- The idea is older than today's chatbots. A 2017 research model called pix2code learned to generate code for iOS, Android and web from a single screenshot of an interface, with over 77% accuracy. That score counted matching code tokens, not whether the page looked right.
- In 2024, researchers tested AI models on 484 real webpages in a benchmark called Design2Code. Human judges said GPT-4V's rebuilt pages could replace the originals in 49% of cases.
- Complex pages are still hard. On a set of 80 harder webpages (Design2Code-HARD), every model tested scored noticeably worse, and GPT-4o's layout-matching score fell from 93.0 to 56.6.
- Design2Code scores a rebuilt page on several things: whether the page blocks match, the text, where elements sit, the colors, and overall visual similarity to the original screenshot.

sources.title: pix2code: Generating Code from a GUI Screenshot (GitHub)
Design2Code: How Far Are We From Automating Front-End Engineering? (Liner review)
Design2Code: Benchmarking Multimodal Code Generation (Liner review)

prompt.system:
You are the producer of a short-video channel (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Your job in this step: choose how the video will be told, by picking ONE template
from the list you are given. You do not write the video yet.

You get the channel, the video idea and the templates.
Pick the template whose "when to use" fits the idea best; the length matters less.
A template's "needs" are the facts its required scenes are built on. Pick one the idea
can fill with its OWN facts: a rise-to-success story needs a success to show, a how-to
needs steps, a list needs items. If the idea lacks what a template needs, that template
does not fit, however close its topic is.
Never invent a template: answer only with an id from the list.
score: 5 = made for this idea and the idea has every fact it needs, 3 = workable,
1 = nothing in the list fits.
reason: one or two sentences for the creator, in plain English, about this idea.

prompt.system:
You write the opening line (hook) of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts):
the words shown and spoken in the first two seconds, which decide whether people keep watching.

Write THREE different hooks for the idea.
The formulas show openings that have worked: follow one where it fits this idea (fill it
in, do not copy its example) or write your own. formulaId = the formula's id, or null for
a hook of your own.
Fill a formula only with what the idea says: never claim something it does not
(no "I switched from…", no number, no result the idea does not give).
Each hook: one line, at most 12 words, plain spoken English, no hashtags, no emojis.
score: 5 = people stop scrolling, 3 = fine, 1 = weak.

prompt.system:
You write the script of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).

Tell ONE connected story. The idea may be written as loose thoughts in any order: sort
them into the order the template's scenes tell (the problem before the fix, the cause
before the result), and let every scene follow from the one before it – the voiceovers
read in a row must make sense as one spoken text. A scene that promises something ("what I learned", "here's why") is
followed by the scene that says it.

The template is a guide: a structure that has worked for videos like this – its scenes,
their order and how they link. Follow it where it serves this idea; change the order,
leave a scene out or add one when that tells this story better. A "repeatable" scene
may appear several times in a row (one per step or item). Put every template scene you
leave out in "skipped" with a short reason.
A scene's "facts" come from the idea and the facts found online only – never invent a
tool, a number or a result.
When the idea has no fact for a scene, leave it out if it is optional; if it is required,
fill it with what the idea does say rather than with an invented claim.
Its "creative" parts are yours to word.

The first scene is the hook: say the chosen hook as it is, and show its key words.
The template's links ("→ next") and the transition phrases are examples of how scenes
can follow each other; use them only where they read naturally. End the way that fits
this video best: the CTA formulas show endings that have worked – use one, or write
your own, or none if no ending asks for one.
The call to action never sends people to a link, a website, a download or a giveaway
the idea does not mention – then pick a CTA formula that needs none of those.

For every scene:
- voiceover: what is said, natural spoken English
- onScreen: the key words shown big, not the whole sentence
- visual: what the viewer sees, concrete (a terminal running a command, a settings page,
  an app icon), never "something engaging"
- needsRecording: your call – true when the scene is shown best with the creator's own
  screen recording rather than a picture the video editor draws.

Keep within the limits. Each scene lasts about as long as its voiceover: fill the wanted
length – add more steps or items with the repeatable scenes, keep the optional scenes
that help – rather than stopping short.

Hook: I gave an AI agent one screenshot. It built this page.

Template: Build it fast – Show the finished thing, then every step that built it
Scenes:
- opening / hook (2–5 s): Shows or names the result and how little time it takes. [required] → next: sequence; facts: result, time, tool-name
- core / demo (4–8 s): Shows one build step on screen. [required] [repeatable] → next: sequence; facts: step, screen-recording
- climax / proof (3.4–5.8 s): Shows the finished thing working. [optional] → next: sequence; facts: result-shot
- close / cta (9–9 s): Offers the link or guide. [optional] → next: none; facts: resource

Transition phrases:
- sequence: First, | Second, | Third, | First is | Second is | Third is

CTA formulas (types allowed: none, comment-keyword):
- comment-keyword: Comment [KEYWORD] and I'll send you [the link / my ebook]. (e.g. "Comment HUMAN and I'll send you my ebook")
- comment-keyword: Comment [KEYWORD] and I'll send you [resource]. Make sure you follow [channel]. (e.g. "Comment HUMAN and I'll send you my ebook. Make sure you follow InsiderForce.")
- comment-keyword: Drop a comment if you want more [topic] with [tool]. (e.g. "Drop a comment if you want more trading ideas with Claude.")

Limits, from the analysis of successful videos:
- speak at most 3.4 words per second
- a scene lasts at most 9 s, the hook at most 5 s
- at most 15 words on screen in a scene

prompt.system:
You lay out the scenes of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Every layout example is taken from a successful video. For every scene, pick ONE
example from that scene's list (layoutExampleId) and fill each of its pictures, in
the order they are listed (fills):
- a logo or prop picture: an id from Logos or Props (both are icons from the library)
- any other picture (a recording, a screen, a photo, a phone): one short sentence
  telling the user what to record or capture there for this scene.
Pick the example whose arrangement suits what the scene shows. When a scene is
marked "own recording: yes", prefer an example with a recording or screen; when it is
marked "own recording: no", prefer an example whose pictures are all logos or props
(nothing to capture), if its list has one.
Answer with one entry per scene, in the same order.

Show how a developer provides a screenshot of a website to an AI agent, which analyzes its visual structure, identifies UI elements, colors, spacing, typography and layout, then generates the corresponding HTML, CSS and React components. The result is a functional webpage that visually resembles the original design.

Scene 1 (hook) – own recording: yes
  On screen: ONE screenshot → THIS page
  Shows: Split screen: on the left a static screenshot of a website landing page, on the right the rebuilt page running live in a browser, with the cursor scrolling it
  Examples:
  - hook-02: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. The background carries the frame: a striking full-frame illustration of the subject. The hook is split around a huge title: small line above, title in the middle, small line below, all centred.
  - hook-04: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; 2 logo → a logo or prop id; 3 logo → a logo or prop id; 4 logo → a logo or prop id; with text. Result on top, how it was made below. The tool logos zigzag left, right, left at different sizes instead of sitting in a row, which keeps the lower half lively; they are the list the video will go through.
  - hook-05: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; with text. A silent visual hook: no captions, no headline over the frame. The opening animation (the laptop opening, the screen lighting up) is the hook; the dark vignette puts all the light on the screen.
  - hook-07: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. Topic on top, a funny picture in the middle, the twist below: the same sandwich as hook-02 but light and playful. A serious topic plus a silly promise ('explained by ducks') is the curiosity gap. Plain white background, nothing else.
  - hook-08: pictures: 1 image → a sentence: what to capture; 2 image → a sentence: what to capture; with text. How to use landscape material in 9:16: the sharp photo across the middle, and behind it the same photo zoomed to fill the frame and heavily blurred, so there are no black bars and the colours match. A meme character adds the emotion; the quote is the hook.

Scene 2 (demo) – own recording: yes
  On screen: 1. Drop the screenshot in
Multimodal = reads images + text
  Shows: Screen recording: the website screenshot is dragged into the AI agent's chat window and a short prompt is typed asking it to rebuild the page
  Examples:
  - demo-01: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; no text. One big thing to look at: the screen being demonstrated fills most of the frame. Captions sit inside its lower part and stay at the same height for the rest of the video; only the hook had them higher.
  - demo-02: pictures: 1 prop → a logo or prop id; with text. Shows the action as input → working: what you type on top, the tool thinking in the middle. Nothing is shown before it is needed.
  - demo-04: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; no text. The app shown whole, as a tidy card, on a playful background (muted blue with thin hand-drawn lines and a few small yellow stars), so the screenshot does not look like a bare screen grab.
  - demo-05: pictures: 1 browser → a sentence: what to capture; no text. How you use it: the input step. Zooming the browser past the frame's sides makes the prompt readable on a phone; a blurred colourful wallpaper shows above and below.

Scene 5 (proof) – own recording: yes
  On screen: Working page ✓
  Shows: Screen recording: the generated page opened in the browser, side by side with the original screenshot, buttons hovering and the page scrolling
  Examples:
  - proof-01: pictures: 1 browser → a sentence: what to capture; 2 image → a sentence: what to capture; no text. A full page is too much to read in a few seconds; a finger on screen tells the viewer exactly where to look, and moving it walks them through the key spots one by one.
  - proof-02: pictures: 1 recording → a sentence: what to capture; 2 recording → a sentence: what to capture; 3 recording → a sentence: what to capture; no text. A gallery of results: three finished examples, each a rounded 16:9 card playing its animation, stacked top to bottom with even gaps, on a dark background with soft orange and blue glows. Three different styles prove the tool is not one-trick.
  - proof-03: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; 2 screen → a sentence: what to capture; with text. Before / after stacked vertically: two identical cards, one word above each, white background, nothing else. Same size and position for both is what makes the change obvious. TikMaker's comparison scene puts the two side by side; on 9:16 stacking gives each card more width.
  - proof-04: pictures: 1 screen → a sentence: what to capture; with text. Credibility beat: the real thing, then one sentence saying why to trust it. White background, the channel watermark at about y 86, lots of empty space under the text.
